--- title: "When the power function is not an error bar" date: 2026-05-14 description: "A note on why kernel power functions do not become pointwise error estimates without a meaningful RKHS norm bound." categories: [notes] jupyter: python3 execute: echo: false warning: false message: false freeze: auto format: html: toc: true toc-location: left toc-depth: 2 anchor-sections: false smooth-scroll: false --- *Status: research note; not peer reviewed. The power-function bound is a standard fact from kernel approximation theory; the experiments below are small diagnostics about why its direct interpretation as a pointwise machine-learning error bar can become vacuous.* A recurring trap in kernel methods is that a computable geometric quantity can look like an uncertainty estimate. The power function is such a quantity. It is mathematically meaningful. It measures how well the design points constrain evaluation at a new point, relative to a chosen kernel. But the usual pointwise error bound is not a power-function-only statement. It has a hidden constant: $$ |f(x)-s_X f(x)| \leq P_X(x)\,\|f\|_{\mathcal H}. $$ The computable part is $P_X(x)$. The difficult part is $\|f\|_{\mathcal H}$. In classical approximation theory this is natural: one assumes that the target belongs to the native space and has controlled norm. In machine learning, the target is unknown, noisy observations are common, the kernel is a modeling choice, and the RKHS norm may be enormous, infinite, or simply not connected to the prediction problem. I use four small diagnostics. - The same power function can accompany very different pointwise errors. - Smooth-looking targets can have very different native-space costs under the same kernel. - The fitted interpolation norm can mostly measure the cost of fitting noise. - The resulting bound can be much larger than the output scale. ## The formal statement Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ be interpolation sites, and let $k$ be a positive definite kernel with RKHS $\mathcal H$. The kernel interpolant has the form $$ s_X f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i k(x,x_i), \qquad K_X\alpha=f_X, $$ where $(K_X)_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)$ and $f_X=(f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_n))^\top$. The power function is $$ P_X^2(x) = k(x,x)-k_X(x)^\top K_X^{-1}k_X(x), $$ where $$ k_X(x)=(k(x,x_1),\ldots,k(x,x_n))^\top. $$ It depends on the kernel, the design, and the evaluation point. It does not depend on the observed values of the target. The standard deterministic estimate is $$ |f(x)-s_X f(x)| \leq P_X(x)\,\|f\|_{\mathcal H}. $$ This is a useful theorem. But the theorem is not the applied statement that $P_X(x)$ is an error bar. A better separation is $$ P_X(x) = \text{design geometry under the kernel}, $$ while $$ \|f\|_{\mathcal H} = \text{unknown target complexity under the kernel}. $$ The second term is usually where the statistical difficulty lives. ## Setup The examples use a one-dimensional Gaussian kernel. This is only for visualization. The point is not specific to this implementation. ## Same power function, different errors Fix the training sites and the kernel. Then the power function is fixed. Now change only the target. ::: {.narrow-figure} ::: {#cell-fig-same-power-different-errors .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Same design and same kernel. The power function is unchanged, but the actual interpolation error depends strongly on the target.](index_files/figure-html/fig-same-power-different-errors-output-1.png){#fig-same-power-different-errors width=650 height=364} ::: ::: ::: The design has not changed. The kernel has not changed. The power function has not changed. Only the target changed. That is enough to rule out the interpretation of $P_X(x)$ alone as a pointwise error estimate. At most, it is the computable geometric factor in a bound whose missing factor is the target norm. Table 1 reports the numerical version of Figure 1. Since the design and kernel are fixed, max power is identical for every target. The changing columns show that the actual error depends on the target and on the relevant norm scale, not on the power function alone. Here, the fitted norm is the computable interpolation norm $\|s_X\|_{\mathcal H}$, and bound scale means $\max_x P_X(x)\,\|s_X\|_{\mathcal H}$. This is a diagnostic scale, not the theorem's true bound with the unknown $\|f\|_{\mathcal H}$. Therefore it can be smaller than the actual error. ::: {#tbl-same-power .cell tbl-cap='Same power function, different target errors. With the same design and kernel, max power is unchanged, while actual interpolation error and fitted norm vary strongly across targets.' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
target max power max error fit norm bound scale vacuity ratio
smooth 0.000301 4.82e-05 1.8 0.000541 0.00027
oscillatory 0.000301 3.78 4.95e+04 14.9 7.46
kink 0.000301 0.032 1.57 0.000474 0.000948
jump 0.000301 0.494 152 0.0458 0.0458
``` ::: ::: ## The hidden norm can become the whole problem Suppose we accept the chosen kernel and ask how expensive different targets are under it. We use a finite-dimensional proxy: $$ \|f\|_{\mathcal H,m}^{2} = f(Z)^\top K_Z^{-1}f(Z), $$ where $Z$ is a fine grid. This is the RKHS norm of the minimum-norm interpolant through the values of $f$ on $Z$. It is not the true continuous RKHS norm of $f$. It is only a diagnostic. But it is useful: if this proxy grows rapidly as the grid is refined, then the native-space assumption is not giving a stable scale for the target. ::: {.narrow-figure} ::: {#cell-fig-norm-proxy-resolution .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Finite-dimensional native-space norm proxy as the grid is refined. The same smooth Gaussian kernel makes oscillatory or nonsmooth targets expensive.](index_files/figure-html/fig-norm-proxy-resolution-output-1.png){#fig-norm-proxy-resolution width=639 height=353} ::: ::: ::: For compatible smooth targets, the scale can remain moderate. For rough, oscillatory, or discontinuous targets, the native-space cost can become very large. The point is not that the theorem fails. The point is that the theorem asks for a target-complexity constant that the machine-learning problem usually does not provide. ::: {#tbl-norm-proxy .cell tbl-cap='Finite-grid RKHS norm proxy versus grid resolution. The smooth target remains stable, while oscillatory, kinked, and discontinuous targets become increasingly expensive under the same Gaussian kernel.' execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
grid size jump kink oscillatory smooth

80 6609.07 133.37 35970.28 1.82
120 8166.49 166.97 40459.34 1.83
180 10020.30 204.79 45304.34 1.83
``` ::: ::: ## A noisy ML-style example In machine learning we usually do not observe a noiseless function. We observe data. A tempting substitution is to replace the unknown $\|f\|_{\mathcal H}$ by the fitted interpolation norm $$ \|s_X\|_{\mathcal H}^{2}=y^\top K_X^{-1}y. $$ This quantity is computable. But it is not the unknown target norm. It is a data-dependent interpolation norm. This quantity is computable. But it is not the unknown target norm. It is a data-dependent interpolation norm. When the noise variance is not negligible relative to the signal, the interpolant is forced to pass through the noise, and the resulting fitted norm can be much larger than the norm of the underlying signal. ::: {.narrow-figure} ::: {#cell-fig-noisy-fitted-norm .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Interpolating noisy observations can make the fitted RKHS norm unstable. The computable fitted norm is not the unknown target norm.](index_files/figure-html/fig-noisy-fitted-norm-output-1.png){#fig-noisy-fitted-norm width=617 height=353} ::: ::: ::: If ridge regularization is introduced, the fitted norm can be stabilized. But then the original interpolation theorem is no longer being used as stated. One has moved from a deterministic interpolation bound to a different regularized statistical procedure. That may be reasonable. It is just not the same certificate. ## Vacuity ratios A bound is useful only if its scale is meaningful relative to the prediction problem. Define the simple diagnostic $$ V = \frac{\max_x P_X(x) C}{\operatorname{range}(y)}, $$ where $C$ is a candidate norm scale. If $C=\|f\|_{\mathcal H}$, this is the formal native-space constant. In practice $C$ is usually unavailable. If one replaces it with a fitted norm or a finite-grid proxy, the number should be interpreted only as a scale diagnostic, not as a theorem. ::: {#tbl-vacuity-ratios .cell tbl-cap='Vacuity ratios for candidate norm scales. The ratios compare the scale of the power-function bound with the output range when using either the fitted interpolation norm or the finite-grid norm proxy.' execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
target max power output range fit norm grid norm proxy V, fit norm V, grid norm
smooth 0.000301 2 1.8 1.83 0.00027 0.000276
oscillatory 0.000301 2 4.95e+04 4.05e+04 7.46 6.09
kink 0.000301 0.499 1.57 167 0.000948 0.101
jump 0.000301 1 152 8.17e+03 0.0458 2.46
``` ::: ::: When these ratios are much larger than one, the bound may be formally true but no longer informative at the scale of the prediction problem. This is the sense in which the norm term becomes vacuous: not because the power function is wrong, but because the hidden complexity factor is too large, too unstable, or unavailable. ## What the power function sees The power function sees: - the kernel - the design points - geometric coverage under the kernel metric - where interpolation is weakly constrained by the data locations The power function does not see: - the unknown target complexity - misspecification of the kernel class - observation noise - distribution shift - model-selection error - hyperparameter-selection error - whether the fitted norm is signal or noise - whether the target belongs to the native space at all This is why the object is useful as a design diagnostic but fragile as a pointwise uncertainty statement. ## The misleading substitution The tempting applied substitution is $$ |f(x)-s_X f(x)| \leq P_X(x)\,\|f\|_{\mathcal H} \qquad\leadsto\qquad \text{error at }x \approx P_X(x). $$ But this removes the factor that depends on the target. A slightly less naive substitution is $$ \|f\|_{\mathcal H} \approx \|s_X\|_{\mathcal H}. $$ This is also not a theorem. It can be a heuristic, but it is data-dependent and can be dominated by noise, conditioning, and hyperparameters. The formal theorem controls approximation error for functions in the RKHS. The machine-learning problem is usually to learn an unknown target from finite, noisy data under model uncertainty. These are not the same problem. ## Takeaway The power function is a valid geometric quantity. It tells us something real about the design and the kernel. But the pointwise error bound is a product: $$ \text{pointwise error} \leq \text{design geometry} \times \text{unknown target complexity}. $$ In applications, the first term is computable and visually appealing. The second term is usually unknown, unstable, or incompatible with the modeling assumptions. A cautious interpretation is therefore: > The power function is a geometry-of-information diagnostic. It is not, without a meaningful and calibrated control of $\|f\|_{\mathcal H}$, a pointwise prediction-error estimate. ## References Gregory E. Fasshauer. *Meshfree Approximation Methods with MATLAB*. World Scientific, 2007. Holger Wendland. *Scattered Data Approximation*. Cambridge University Press, 2005. Robert Schaback and Holger Wendland. “Kernel techniques: From machine learning to meshless methods.” *Acta Numerica* 15, 2006. Carl Edward Rasmussen and Christopher K. I. Williams. *Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning*. MIT Press, 2006. ## Suggested citation ```bibtex @misc{miryusupov2026powerfunction, author = {Miryusupov, Shohruh}, title = {When the Power Function Is Not an Error Bar}, year = {2026}, howpublished = {Research note}, url = {https://www.miryusupov.com/blog/posts/power_function_not_error_bar/index.html} } ```
